title: The Space Before Yes
subtitle: When every request becomes your responsibility, make room for a thoughtful answer.
topic: WHEN EVERY REQUEST BECOMES YOUR RESPONSIBILITY

benefits: For one non-urgent request, replace an immediate yes with a specific time when you will answer.
Turn one vague offer of help into a specific contribution you could finish.
Check one overdue promise. Send an honest update with a date you can support.
ideas: A pause is part of an answer
Offer a smaller true yes
Repair the promise you cannot keep
facts.everyday: A request can arrive as a small favour and leave as a permanent obligation. This book explores the moment before an answer becomes a commitment. It asks how generosity, limits and responsibility can belong in the same life. Boundaries are not a technique for making everyone pleased with you. They are practical arrangements that let people understand what you can offer and what they need to decide for themselves. Begin with one ordinary request, rather than trying to redesign every relationship at once.
facts.theme: When every request becomes your responsibility, make room for a thoughtful answer.

captions: A pause is part of an answer

title: Think Again, Gently
subtitle: When being wrong feels personal, learn to revise a belief without losing yourself.

benefits: Write a contested belief without using a sentence that begins with the kind of person I am.
Label one current judgment tentative, reasonably supported or strongly supported, then state the evidence.
Ask who relied on a claim you no longer support. Update those people directly.
ideas: A belief is not your whole identity
Confidence can have degrees
Change publicly enough to repair the effect
facts.everyday: A changed mind is often described as a defeat. It can also be an act of care for what is true. This book explores ordinary situations in which a belief becomes entangled with identity, belonging or pride. Its aim is neither permanent doubt nor automatic agreement with whoever sounds most certain. It is a more usable relationship with reasons: state what you think, examine what supports it, and allow the strength of your commitment to match the strength of the evidence.
facts.theme: When being wrong feels personal, learn to revise a belief without losing yourself.

captions: A belief is not your whole identity

title: The Quiet Art of Enough
subtitle: When comparison keeps moving the finish line, decide what a good life actually needs.
topic: WHEN COMPARISON KEEPS MOVING THE FINISH LINE

benefits: Before one purchase, write the specific job you need it to do.
Choose three necessary criteria for one ordinary decision. Stop searching when a credible option meets them.
Identify one shared resource where your convenience creates a cost for someone else.
ideas: Name the purpose before the quantity
A stopping rule protects another value
Leave room for other people
facts.everyday: Enough is not a universal quantity. It is a question about purpose, need and the kind of life you are trying to support. A person facing insecurity may need more resources, not a lesson in wanting less. A person who already has room may still experience every gain as unfinished. This book explores that second difficulty without erasing the first. It asks how a chosen standard can interrupt comparison, make enjoyment possible and leave room for responsibilities beyond acquisition.
facts.theme: When comparison keeps moving the finish line, decide what a good life actually needs.

captions: Name the purpose before the quantity
A stopping rule protects another value

title: When Life Changes
subtitle: When the old plan no longer fits, find a thoughtful way to begin again.
topic: WHEN THE OLD PLAN NO LONGER FITS

benefits: Make three short lists: changed, unchanged and not yet known.
Turn one large uncertainty into a question you could investigate this week.
Write two feelings and the part of the situation each one concerns.
ideas: Describe the change before naming its meaning
Choose the next useful question
Allow mixed feelings to remain mixed
facts.everyday: A change can interrupt more than a plan. It can disturb the roles, expectations and familiar explanations through which a day made sense. This book offers questions for finding a next step without pretending that every disruption is a hidden gift. Some losses need grief, practical help or professional support rather than a better interpretation. Reflection can accompany those needs. It can help distinguish what has ended, what remains uncertain and what is still possible to care for today.
facts.theme: When the old plan no longer fits, find a thoughtful way to begin again.

captions: Describe the change before naming its meaning

title: Meditations, Reimagined
subtitle: Meet a difficult day with clearer judgment, steadier action and room for other people.
author: Marcus Aurelius
topic: MEET A DIFFICULT DAY WITH CLEARER JUDGMENT

benefits: Name one predictable difficulty and prepare a proportionate response before it arrives.
Name the people who benefit from a decision and the people who carry its burden.
Separate your preparation, other people’s choices and external conditions in one outcome.
ideas: Meet the day before you judge it
Remember the larger company
Keep your part proportionate
facts.everyday: Marcus Aurelius wrote the notes now called Meditations as reminders to himself, not as a finished system for other people. They return to judgment, duty, change and belonging to a larger world. This companion follows eight of those concerns through contemporary situations. It does not ask you to copy a Roman emperor’s circumstances or accept every part of Stoic cosmology. Read the source alongside the guide, and distinguish Marcus’s ancient arguments from the practical exercises OPortals proposes today.

captions: Meet the day before you judge it

title: Epictetus: A Freer Mind
subtitle: When the outcome is uncertain, distinguish your next choice from what you cannot command.
author: Epictetus

benefits: List what you can decide, what you can influence and what remains external in one situation.
Write one hope, then remove any hidden claim that the outcome must be guaranteed.
Choose a low-stakes situation to rehearse one considered response for three days.
ideas: Separate direction from possession
Desire can ask for an impossible contract
Practise before the difficult moment
facts.everyday: The Enchiridion is a short handbook drawn by Arrian from the teaching of Epictetus. It begins with a distinction between what is up to us and what is not. This companion explores that distinction through judgments, roles and ordinary pressures. It also names a limit of simple modern summaries: political exclusion, illness and material harm are not solved by telling a person to adjust their attitude. The exercises concern thoughtful agency within circumstances, alongside appropriate action to change those circumstances.

captions: Desire can ask for an impossible contract

title: Epicurus: The Art of Enough
subtitle: Explore pleasure, friendship and the difference between a need and an endless demand.
author: Epicurus
sourceTitle: Letter to Menoeceus and Principal Doctrines

benefits: Choose one desire and name the need, enjoyment or social comparison it contains.
Give one ordinary purchase a stopping rule based on its purpose.
Try a modest version of an enjoyment and notice what it preserves and what it changes.
ideas: Begin with the desire
A limit can make enjoyment possible
Simple need not mean joyless
facts.everyday: Epicurus is often reduced to a name for luxurious pleasure. His surviving Letter to Menoeceus and Principal Doctrines invite a more demanding reading: examine desires, consider consequences and attend to friendship and freedom from disturbance. This companion offers contemporary exercises inspired by those themes. It is not a clinical guide to pain or anxiety and does not claim that hardship is solved by simplicity. Ancient arguments about nature and death are presented as arguments to examine, not beliefs you must accept.
facts.theme: Letter to Menoeceus and Principal Doctrines

captions: A limit can make enjoyment possible

title: Plato: The Examined Life
subtitle: Ask better questions about what you know, what you value and the life you are practising.
author: Plato
topic: ASK BETTER QUESTIONS ABOUT WHAT YOU KNOW

benefits: Name one area where your confidence extends beyond the reasons you can currently give.
Identify one rewarded habit and the kind of conduct it is making easier.
Separate a feared future into a known risk, a plausible possibility and an unsupported certainty.
ideas: Begin where certainty becomes difficult
Care for the way you become
Ignorance about the future has limits
facts.everyday: Plato’s Apology presents Socrates defending himself before an Athenian jury. It is a dramatic philosophical text, not a neutral transcript of the trial. Socrates examines reputation, knowledge, civic duty and the value of questioning a life. This companion follows selected passages through contemporary situations. It does not turn questioning into a licence to humiliate people or treat Socrates as the final authority on every ethical problem. Read the dialogue for its arguments, tensions and particular setting.

captions: Care for the way you become

title: Aristotle: A Life of Character
subtitle: Explore how habits, judgment and friendship shape a life beyond its achievements.
author: Aristotle

benefits: Trace one goal through two questions of what it is for. Notice where the answer becomes less clear.
Identify an excess, a deficiency and a fitting response in one ordinary situation.
Offer a friend attention that is not a disguised request for a service.
ideas: Ask what the achievement is for
The mean is not the middle of every dispute
Friendship can value the person
facts.everyday: The Nicomachean Ethics asks about human flourishing and the activities, relationships and conditions through which it becomes possible. Aristotle connects character with repeated action, but does not reduce ethics to an individual habit tracker. Circumstances and external goods also matter. This companion examines selected ideas while acknowledging that Aristotle’s ancient social assumptions include exclusions contemporary readers should criticise. It offers original examples and exercises, not a complete account of his ethics or an endorsement of every conclusion.

captions: Ask what the achievement is for

title: Seneca: On the Shortness of Life
subtitle: When being busy feels like living, ask where your time and attention are actually going.
author: Seneca
sourceTitle: On the Shortness of Life (De brevitate vitae)
topic: WHEN BEING BUSY FEELS LIKE LIVING

benefits: Choose one recurring commitment and write the purpose it currently serves.
Choose one period of rest and reduce one competing demand where you reasonably can.
Choose one available act of care that you would regret repeatedly postponing.
ideas: Busyness does not explain its purpose
Rest can inherit the same restlessness
Keep mortality practical and humane
facts.everyday: Seneca’s On the Shortness of Life examines the difference between having years and making a life of them. Addressed to Paulinus, it criticises forms of busyness through the perspective of a wealthy Roman writer. This companion does not assume that people facing insecure work or care duties can simply choose leisure. It uses Seneca’s questions to examine the choices that are available, the obligations that are real and the social conditions that restrict the room a person has.
facts.theme: On the Shortness of Life (De brevitate vitae)
